rationale: Premise states cutting forces are higher than in surgery, but does not mention machining explicitly or claim greater structural rigidity is required.
Premise only notes unspecified chip evacuation problems. Hypothesis adds context (continuum-robot machining, confined geometries) and a limitation claim not stated in the premise.
Hypothesis generalizes “usually” to all CNC machines and adds a causal claim about accurate positioning not explicitly stated in the premise.
The premise states 0.005" is “really sloppy” by machining tolerances, which entails it is very loose by typical machining standards.
Premise asserts speed is essential to making money in CNC machining, supporting that cycle time/speed dominates economics and is critical for profitability.
Premise supports deformation-based movement and slower speed, but does not mention task durations or machining contexts. The hypothesis adds that they take longer for tasks.
Premise refers to unspecified devices lacking rigidity; hypothesis specifies continuum robots and machining generally. Added specificity not stated in the premise, so not entailed.
Premise says continuum robots usually require such components and are high-cost; hypothesis claims inherent necessity and adds machining deployment costs, which the premise does not state.
Hypothesis restates the premise: milling/turning need very high rigidity to control cutting forces and ensure machining/dimensional accuracy. No added unsupported details.
Premise notes no good way to meet machining tolerances but doesn’t mention continuum robots, CNC, or label it a fundamental limitation. Added context not supported.
Paraphrase match: CNC needs sub-millimeter repeatability; continuum robots struggle to maintain it due to compliant/flexible structures and drive mechanisms.
Premise states continuum robots lack economic advantages in machining speed and system integration versus rigid CNC; the hypothesis is a faithful paraphrase.
Premise states nonlinear flexible drives in continuum robots hinder path/toolpath planning, force control, and dynamic compensation for CNC, matching the hypothesis’ claims.
Premise mentions instability during cutting and unspecified errors. Hypothesis generalizes to machining, specifies cutting loads, and claims dimensional errors—details not stated in the premise.
Premise states a ring may not need radial tension, but doesn’t specify retaining rings, general-duty applications, or functional adequacy. Added scope and purpose make it neutral.
Premise supports smaller free ID causing tension when installed, but doesn’t specify external rings/shafts or that preload provides the retaining force.
Premise states no heat is generated or it’s removed by fluid, but does not mention abrasive waterjet, “cool machining,” or explicitly avoiding thermal effects.
Premise states no contact and disregards hardness, but hypothesis adds comparison to conventional cutting and effectiveness claims not explicit in the premise.
The hypothesis rephrases the premise’s definition using synonymous terms (“deepest cut”/“greatest depth”; “one pass”/“single pass”). No extra claims are introduced.
Premise supports differing EDM rates and relative speeds for copper, aluminum, and lead, but does not specify wire EDM; adding that detail exceeds the premise.
Premise states a too-deep (small-diameter) groove lets the ring sink enough for something to slide off, matching the hypothesis’ assertion about retained components.
Premise only states tolerances for grooves to be cut. Hypothesis adds specifics about catalog labels, shaft/snap ring context, and exclusion of ring dimensions not mentioned.
Premise states each machine has a safe maximum cutting depth without damage or harm, directly matching the hypothesis’ claim.
Premise says if depth needed exceeds max, use multiple passes removing some material each time—exactly what the hypothesis states.
Premise states an overly wide groove lets the ring tilt and be twisted off, matching the hypothesis that excessive width enables removal and defeats retention.
Premise states shallower depth reduces machine stress and necessitates more passes. Hypothesis restates this trade-off without adding details. Fully supported.
Premise states travel speed equals feed per rev times spindle speed, but does not mention using it for time calculations. Extra claim not supported.
Premise states McMaster-Carr lists recommended groove and ring/groove tolerances to reference. Hypothesis advises consulting these listings for such tolerances; purpose is implicit.
Premise advises not assuming nominal thickness and to consider tolerance and desired fit, which supports adjusting groove spacing rather than using nominal width.
Premise says cutting too much causes dig-in and possible damage, but does not specify depth of cut. Hypothesis adds that specific detail.
Premise supports hands-on calibration and understanding lever-arm amplification, but does not state a contrast with ‘relying only on numbers.’ That added claim isn’t explicit.
The premise explicitly computes spindle speed using n = v/(π·d) with units and values, directly matching the hypothesis formula.
Premise only says reducing depth allows adjusting cutting speed, without specifying higher speeds or conditions. Hypothesis adds direction (“higher”) and dependencies not stated.
Premise notes radius reduction and a specific total longitudinal cut (3 mm). Hypothesis generalizes to diameter-vs-radius (X → X/2) and measurement convention not stated.
Premise is vague and domain-agnostic. Hypothesis adds machining context, a workflow (start high-level), and conditional use of physics not stated in the premise.
Premise states drilling removes a cylindrical void centered at (x,y) with diameter d; hypothesis restates this geometric subtraction. No added details or contradictions.
Premise states most tools lack models, but says nothing about predictive simulations or practitioner reliance. The hypothesis adds these consequences, so it’s not entailed.
Premise states machining models exist at multiple abstraction levels, but does not claim that the appropriate level depends on the questions being answered.
Premise advises measuring easily verifiable features, preferring mirror entities and diameters over centerlines/radii, matching the hypothesis’s guidance for inspection-friendly dimensions.
Premise shows r=d/2 and t=r/ẋ, but does not mention parting or the necessity of traversing from OD to centerline.
Premise states geometric models don’t determine feed/rotation rates and require a lower-level model. Hypothesis restates this; example model types don’t add required claims.
Premise supports measuring from the centerline when it’s important, but does not mention datums or design intent. The added generalization is unstated.
Premise only says flipping may cause tolerance issues. Hypothesis adds specifics (second setup, alignment/stack-up, failing stated tolerances) not stated in the premise.
If computers need formal representations to understand geometric objects, then computational reasoning about machining parts (geometric objects) also requires formal, not informal, representations.
Premise states dimensions are for humans and software already knows geometry, implying annotations (e.g., baseline vs centerline) don’t affect how the model is understood.
Premise recommends examining and disassembling mini lathes, but doesn’t claim they’re ‘proven’ or that this avoids heavy theoretical modeling. Added rationale isn’t supported.
Premise states machining causes deformation that creates residual stresses on the surface, matching the hypothesis about surface-concentrated residual stresses from machining-induced deformation.
Premise supports lower concern for loads/vibrations in hobby plastic-cutting. It doesn’t mention modeling prioritization or compare to industrial machines, which the Hypothesis adds.
Premise says consider automatic vs human-guided operation order only after final design. This supports deferring sequencing to CAM/human guidance post-design, not during drawing.
Premise only says the document serves as acceptance criteria if things go wrong. Hypothesis adds specifics about drawings, contractual status, and tolerances not stated.
Premise supports matching baseline referencing, but does not mention reasons like tolerance stack-up. The hypothesis adds causal details not stated in the premise.
Premise supports uneven face removal causing warp on thinner plates (<1 inch) but does not specify aluminum. The material-specific detail is added by the Hypothesis.
Premise only states the machine may not be rigid enough; it does not mention distortion, flatness, or machining outcomes. The causal claim is added.
Premise mentions referencing centerlines to minimize tolerance but doesn’t specify a square pattern, baselines, or first locating two holes. Added procedural details aren’t stated.
Premise supports that wrong feeds/speeds stop chips removing heat, but does not mention distortion or its likelihood. Added consequence is not entailed.
Premise supports a grain size gradient from outer to inner due to cooling and roller compression, but does not specify aluminum or plate, making added details unsupported.
The premise states an unspecified “it” is mainly used to clean rust off a casting; it doesn’t specify sand blasting. The hypothesis adds that detail.
Premise says to keep coolant below 28°C. Hypothesis adds a causal reason (controls cutting heat), which isn’t stated in the premise.
Premise explicitly states the same procedure and purpose: skim, flip, break skin, then ~0.005 in spring cut with vice opened and light clamping for unstressed flatness.
Premise only states heat is generated during machining due to shearing force. It doesn’t specify tool–work interface or coolant removal, which the Hypothesis adds.
Premise is conditional and lacks mention of abrasive jet machining; hypothesis asserts an unconditional, process-specific and interpretive claim about capability differences.
Premise supports coating, mating, spotting, scraping, and repeating, but does not state achieving uniform contact or that it yields precise fits without gauges.
Premise explicitly advises never using AJM to clean casting threads due to potential damage, matching the hypothesis’s caution about damaging the thread form.
Premise states interchangeability for mass manufacture requires standardized measurement and tolerances, implying without them parts won’t reliably substitute. Hypothesis restates this necessity.
Premise states machinable wax has a bit more strength than paraffin. It doesn’t mention temporary filler use, added rigidity needs, or being a better choice.
Premise mentions casting into a bearing and hand scraping to fit a shaft, but doesn’t specify Babbitt, precision level, or lack of precision machines.
Premise states prioritizing relative fit over absolute measurements and that high absolute accuracy isn’t necessary, which directly matches the hypothesis.
Premise only states PVC soldering rod didn’t stick. Hypothesis adds specifics (aluminum slot, temporary filler, rigidity purpose) not supported by the Premise.
Premise states sandblasting lacks velocity and has too large a jet for accurate machining, especially for intricate shapes in brittle materials—matching the hypothesis’ claims.
Premise states reducing tool diameter reduces cutting force, which supports using smaller diameter tools to lower cutting load during machining.
Premise only suggests Wood’s metal as a low-melting filler during machining. Hypothesis adds context (machinable wax, thin sections, easy melt-out) not stated.
Premise says lapping/honing tend to yield precise flats/bores without precision tools. Hypothesis adds a self-correcting mechanism and stronger certainty (“very true”), not stated.
Premise claims measurements can exceed instrument precision, but gives no method. Hypothesis adds specific techniques (geometric references, simple tools) and applications, which aren’t stated.
Premise implies non-interchangeability, but does not specify hand-fitting as the approach or discuss standardization/replacement implications. Added details exceed the premise.
The premise only states “10% cadmium content” without mentioning Wood’s metal or standard composition, so the added specificity in the hypothesis isn’t supported.
Premise only states mixing paraffin wax with shredded polythene (15–25%). It doesn’t mention strength, machinability, or that it’s a wax filler.
Premise mentions qualitative maintainability ratings, not machinability, and says nothing about absence of quantitative measures. Thus the hypothesis adds unstated details.
Premise mentions something costing ~$50/lb at flexbar.com as expensive, but doesn’t specify Wood’s metal or characterize “industrial suppliers.”
Premise says work hardening may be easy to mitigate with correct procedures if aware. Hypothesis adds “often” and specifies machining/operator context not stated.
Premise states molten Wood’s metal fills tubes, solidifies to prevent collapse during bending, then is removed by heating, often in boiling water—matching the hypothesis.
Premise mentions a comprehensive rating system and comparisons for aluminum alloys, but does not state it is about machinability or gauging relative machinability.
Premise discusses maintainability; hypothesis claims about machinability and alloys. Different concept and added specifics not supported by the premise.
Premise states long stringy swarf is a major problem in automation but only mildly inconvenient in one-off manual work, matching the hypothesis’ claims.
Premise notes cheaper/safer variants, mostly higher melting points with exceptions like Cerrolow, but it doesn’t specify they’re compared to Wood’s metal.
The premise states many aluminum grades are reasonably machinable and have fewer severe issues than some stainless/high-alloy steels, matching the hypothesis’ claims.
Premise only asserts MO-59’s lead yields smooth cuts. Hypothesis generalizes to all leaded brass and infers a selection strategy, which the premise doesn’t state.
The hypothesis paraphrases the premise: some alloys are easy to rough-machine but resist achieving a fine surface finish. No extra claims added.
Premise supports copper’s poor machining finish vs brass, but does not specify leaded brass. The added ‘leaded’ detail isn’t in the source.
Premise says “it” is less likely than wax to shift, but doesn’t specify Wood’s metal or filler use. The hypothesis adds that unstated detail.
Premise expects 100 of 20 mm parts in one run on most machines, but doesn’t specify DMLS or build volumes. Hypothesis adds that specific context.
Premise states helium in an 8 mm gap can give up to 20 dB suppression, but does not specify the gap is between dual panes.
Premise states nitrile has low helium permeability and will be used to seal windows, implying suitability as a helium-retaining sealant.
Premise describes a powder-bed, layer-by-layer sintering enabling complex shapes with minimal support, but does not specify DMLS/metal nor explicitly state unsintered powder provides support.
